Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the mobility mechanisms of screw and edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) across a wide temperature range?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), specifically comparing random solid solution (RSS) and equilibrium SRO states at 800 K. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a moment tensor potential (MTP) machine-learning interatomic potential; SRO states equilibrated via hybrid MD/Monte Carlo (MD/MC) approach at 800 K. Test conditions: Temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K; applied shear stresses ranging from 0 to 3.0 GPa for screws and 0 to 1.0 GPa for edges; dislocation line length ~15 nm. Findings: At 300 K, SRO provides an extra strengthening of ~180 MPa for screw dislocations due to the formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs).; The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations attenuates with increasing temperature, becoming negligible at 2000 K where mobility curves for RSS and SRO samples overlap.; A cross-slip locking mechanism involving the formation of jogs is observed for screw dislocations, providing extra strengthening independent of SRO presence.; Unlike screw dislocations, the mobility of edge dislocations is enhanced by the presence of SRO, particularly in the high-stress regime.; The SRO-induced enhancement of edge dislocation mobility extends to a characteristic length scale of approximately 1.2 nm into neighboring planes.; At 300 K, dislocation velocities in the MoNbTaW RHEA are significantly lower than in pure Mo and Nb, but this difference diminishes at 2000 K.; The attenuation of SRO strengthening at high temperatures is attributed to the increasing contribution of the entropy term (ΔS_kp) to the kink-pair formation free energy.. Mechanism: For screw dislocations, SRO creates an energy barrier (DAPB formation energy) that must be overcome during kink-pair nucleation, causing strengthening that is thermally activated and thus diminishes at high temperatures. For edge dislocations, SRO flattens the energy landscape, reducing solute drag effects and enhancing mobility despite the energy cost of disrupting order on the slip plane. Cross-slip locking in screws involves the formation of jogs on different slip planes that pin the dislocation line.. Limitations: The simulations use short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm) compared to realistic experimental conditions, meaning calculated velocities are dependent on this size and cannot be directly compared to macroscopic theoretical models without extrapolation. The study assumes the SRO state remains fixed during dislocation motion and does not account for changes in ordering around the moving core.. Future work: The authors state that predicting how the identified mechanisms combine to determine material strength requires appealing to mesoscale models for longer dislocation lengths and longer timescales, which is beyond the scope of the current work.. Quote: "The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced."

Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) and temperature affect the mobility and friction stress of edge versus screw dislocations in a bcc MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) compared to pure bcc metals and binary alloys?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), pure Mo, and binary Mo-Nb alloys (Mo95Nb5 to Mo75Nb25). Processing: Machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) with radius cutoff (Rcut) of 4.7 Å and maximum level (levmax) of 14; MC/MD equilibration at 800 K; dislocation mobility simulations using LAMMPS with shear stress ramped at 20 MPa per 1.5 ps and held for 150 ps at temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K. Test conditions: Temperatures: 300 K and 2000 K; Shear stress ramp rate: 20 MPa per 1.5 ps; Hold time: 150 ps; Critical friction stress defined at 0.2 Å/ps for screw and 1.0 Å/ps for edge dislocations. Findings: The edge-to-screw velocity ratio decreases from 20 at 300 K to 11 at 2000 K in MoNbTaW.; Critical friction stress for edge dislocations decreases by 140 MPa from 300 to 2000 K.; Critical friction stress for screw dislocations decreases by 1.3 GPa (an order of magnitude larger) from 300 to 2000 K.; At ~2000 K, the critical friction stresses for both edge and screw dislocations decay to approximately the same level.; SRO hinders screw dislocation motion but accelerates edge dislocation motion in the RHEA.; A novel cross-slip locking mechanism was observed in the RHEA, attributed to intrinsic energy fluctuations and rugged energy landscapes.; Critical stress for screw dislocations follows an exponential decay with temperature, while edge dislocations follow a linear decrease.; Binary Mo-Nb alloys show lower critical friction stresses compared to the RHEA, with edge friction converging to zero in pure bcc metals.. Mechanism: Screw dislocations move via kink-pair nucleation and migration; SRO increases the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation, causing temperature-dependent strengthening. Edge dislocations are accelerated by SRO through the attenuation of solute interaction magnitudes. The cross-slip locking mechanism arises from intrinsic energy fluctuations along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape.. Limitations: The study notes that the cross-slip locking mechanism was observed even with a limited cell size, implying potential size effects, and the phenomenological model is constructed specifically for the double-kink mechanism.. Future work: The authors state that the findings demonstrate mechanisms that can have a significant impact on mechanical properties, implying future work should explore these impacts, though no specific future experiments are explicitly detailed in the provided text.. Quote: "The edge-to-screw mobility ratio is around 20 at 300 K, which decreases to 11 when the temperature is raised to 2000 K."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the Al concentration (3.5 to 54 at.%) influence phase formation and magnetic properties in FeMnCoCrAl high entropy alloy thin films?. System: FeMnCoCrAl high entropy alloy thin films with Al content varying from 3.5 to 54 at.%. Processing: Co-sputtering of equiatomic FeMn, Co, Cr, and Al targets on Si (100) and Al2O3 (0001) substrates; power density varied from 2 to 7.5 W cm−2 for Al target; base pressure 2 × 10−5 Pa; Ar gas at 0.4 Pa; deposition time 22 min; substrate temperature <80 °C. Test conditions: Room temperature magnetic hysteresis (VSM, 5 T max field), temperature-dependent magnetization (10 mT field), XRD (grazing incidence, Co Kα), EDX, Atom Probe Tomography (60 K, 30 pJ laser pulse), TEM (200 kV), electrical resistivity (four-point probe, Van-der-Pauw method). Findings: Al additions to FeMnCoCr (α-Mn structure) induce formation of a body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, with a single BCC random solid solution forming at 8 at.% Al.; The largest saturation magnetization (Ms) of 82 Am2/kg was measured for the film containing 8 at.% Al.; Increasing Al concentration beyond 8 at.% causes a continuous decrease in Ms, dropping to 37 Am2/kg at 20 at.% Al and 7 Am2/kg at 40 at.% Al.; Thin films with Al concentrations of 26 at.% and 40 at.% exhibit nanoscale chemical separation (Al-Co rich regions) not resolved by standard XRD.; The 8 at.% Al single BCC phase thin film possesses a Curie temperature (Tc) greater than 900 K.; The coercivity (Hc) decreases from 13 mT at 4 at.% Al to 2.1 mT at 40 at.% Al, correlating with a reduction in column width from ~54 nm to ~20 nm.; The single phase BCC film containing 8 at.% Al exhibits an electrical resistivity of 151 µΩ cm, which increases with higher Al concentrations.. Mechanism: Al additions stabilize the BCC phase over the FCC phase by forming a pseudogap at the Fermi level. The increase in Ms at low Al content is due to the formation of the ferromagnetic BCC phase, while the subsequent decrease is caused by the dilution of ferromagnetic species (Fe, Co) by paramagnetic Al and lattice distortions from Al's larger atomic radius. Nanoscale segregation in high-Al films further reduces magnetization by reducing ferromagnetic exchange interactions.. Limitations: The thin film synthesis involves high quenching rates, so the composition boundaries for phase formation might deviate from those obtained by near-equilibrium processing. The study notes that more detailed investigations on factors affecting coercivity and magnetic anisotropy are subject of future work.. Future work: More detailed investigations on factors affecting Hc and the effects of magnetic anisotropy are subject of future work. The authors also suggest the material system may enable applications in magneto-caloric devices or high-frequency inductors.. Quote: "Al additions to FeMnCoCr crystallizing in the alpha-Mn structure cause the formation of the body centered cubic (BCC) structure."

Processing: modified coprecipitation hydrothermal method with quenching in liquid nitrogen, 72 h at 150 °C under autogenous pressure, then heated up to 1200 °C and kept at this temperature for 2 h in an air atmosphere. Test conditions: temperature range from 3 up to 300 K, magnetic field of 100 mT, temperature range from 225 up to 450 K. Findings: The compound exhibits weak ferromagnetism at T ≤ 10 K; Signatures of antiferromagnetic correlations in the paramagnetic phase; A band gap Δ = 1.18 eV in the ground-state electronic structure; A sudden drop in activation energy at T ∼ 240 K from Ea ∼ 1 eV in the low-temperature phase to Ea ∼ 0.3 eV at room temperature; The configuration entropy calculated using eq 1 is equal to 1.61R (0.0134 kJ·mol–1·K–1); The orthorhombic perovskite structure with small (less than 4%) precipitation of the RE2O3 phase; The semiconductor-to-semiconductor transition is related to the evolution of the electronic structure related to structural distortion. Mechanism: The high configuration entropy of the A-site cations is likely responsible for good accommodation of the deformation of CoO6 octahedra by the lattice and thus a lack of sudden structural phase transitions. Future work: Fine tuning of cationic stoichiometry in high-entropy cobalt oxides may be used to optimize the value of activation energy and temperature of phase transition in a wide range required by the different applications of perovskite cobalt oxides. card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?. System: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu. Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV. Findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).; The glass-to-glass transition is irreversible; the heat-treated sample shows a distinct glass transition temperature (Tg) at ~764 K and lacks the first exothermic peak observed in the as-prepared state.; Nanoindentation measurements reveal a drastic increase in hardness from 6.78 GPa to 9.46 GPa (approximately 40% increase) after the transition.; In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows a significant non-linear shift of the first peak in the total structure function S(Q) and a narrowing of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) during the transition.; Pair-distribution function (G(r)) analysis indicates a contraction of short-range atomic distances (r11 and r12 shift to low-r) and prominent splitting of the second peak, signifying enhanced short- and medium-range ordering.; Atom probe tomography confirms a uniform element distribution at the sub-nanometer scale in both as-prepared and heat-treated samples, excluding spinodal decomposition.; The calculated lower limit of entropy change (ΔSH−L) for the transition is −1.96 J mol−1 K−1, with a corresponding enthalpy change (ΔHH−L) of −1.65 kJ mol−1.; Substituting Co with Cu to form NbNiZrTiCu (maintaining high excess configurational entropy) and adding Cu to form NbNiZrTiCoCu both result in similar glass-to-glass transitions.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy (SC) and high excess configurational entropy (SE) dynamically stabilize a high-energy glass state during rapid vitrification by hindering atomic reconstruction and slowing diffusion. Upon heating, this high-energy state undergoes a thermodynamically driven transition to a low-energy, more ordered glass state, releasing a large amount of heat. The transition is driven by the specific combination of high SC and high SE (related to atomic size misfit), which enables the formation of a high-energy glass that is distinct from conventional metallic glasses.. Limitations: The text notes that the observed phase transition is an irreversible process, meaning the calculated entropy change represents a lower limit. Additionally, the detailed structural changes cannot be fully resolved by atom probe tomography due to its limited spatial resolution, and some weak diffraction peaks in crystallized samples could not be identified.. Future work: The authors suggest that the HEMGs may serve as model materials for exploring glass-to-glass transitions and the fundamental nature of glasses in materials science and condensed-matter physics. They also propose potential applications as energetic materials due to the large anomalous exotherm, which could contribute to combustion heats and lower ignition temperatures.. Quote: "An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How can strong local compositional disorder in high entropy oxides be exploited to generate tunable magnetic behaviors, ranging from macroscopically ordered states to frustration-driven dynamic spin interactions, and can a simplified model predict the emergence of these states?. System: La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 (L5BO) and Mn-varied variants La(Cr0.15Mn0.4Fe0.15Co0.15Ni0.15)O3 (40% Mn) and La(Cr0.1Mn0.6Fe0.1Co0.1Ni0.1)O3 (60% Mn). Processing: Pulsed laser epitaxy (PLD) on SrTiO3 (STO) and (La0.3Sr0.7)(Al0.65Ta0.35)O3 (LSAT) substrates; films were single-phase, epitaxial, with thicknesses of 56 nm (40% Mn), 58 nm (60% Mn), 62 nm (20% Mn), and ~90 nm for neutron diffraction.. Test conditions: Neutron diffraction on single-crystal films and bulk powder; SQUID magnetometry (field-cooled vs. zero-field-cooled) from low temperatures up to 300 K; Monte Carlo simulations using a classical Heisenberg model.. Findings: L5BO (20% Mn) exhibits robust long-range G-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering with a Néel temperature (T_N) near 180 K in single-crystal films.; Increasing Mn concentration to 40% creates a degenerate tipping point where both AFM and ferromagnetic (FM) phases are percolated, resulting in a horizontal exchange bias shift.; Increasing Mn concentration to 60% shifts the dominant phase to ferromagnetism with a Curie temperature (T_C) of approximately 160 K and no observable exchange bias.; The 20% Mn system shows a vertical loop shift due to uncompensated FM moments within a percolated AFM matrix.; The 40% Mn composition displays an incipient quantum critical point where AFM and FM signals grow simultaneously upon cooling.; A classical Heisenberg model populated with composite parameter states accurately predicted the magnetic phase diagram and critical temperatures.; Exchange bias behaviors, traditionally found in bilayer heterojunctions, were generated in monolithic single-crystal films by manipulating local spin disorder.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high entropy oxide hosts a random distribution of spin (S) and exchange (J) interactions where the dominant magnetic phase is determined by the percolation of specific microstates. Increasing Mn concentration shifts the balance from AFM-dominant (Fe-O-Fe bonds) to FM-dominant (Mn-O-X bonds). At 40% Mn, the system reaches a state where both AFM and FM clusters percolate coherently, creating intrinsic frustration and uncompensated spins at the interface of these coexisting phases, which drives the exchange bias effect without the need for physical heterostructuring.. Limitations: The text notes that computationally intensive first-principles approaches are impractical for high entropy oxides due to the vast number of possible microstates (over 200 nearest neighbor combinations), necessitating the use of a simplified classical Heisenberg model rather than precise quantitative calculations.. Future work: The authors propose that manipulating local spin disorder can be used to design novel Griffiths phases or quantum many-body systems with tunable critical behaviors, and that replacing geometric frustration with exchange frustration on a square lattice may lead to unexpected phase spaces.. Quote: "Single‐crystal La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 films are used as a model system hosting a magnetic sublattice with a high degree of microstate disorder in the form of site‐to‐site spin and exchange type inhomogeneity."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the conditional entropy of a posterior probability distribution relate to the location error in indoor localization using probabilistic Wi-Fi fingerprinting?. System: Wi-Fi fingerprinting system. Processing: Probabilistic sensor model with various training options and parameters. Test conditions: Three publicly available datasets (EVARILOS, GEOTEC, UJIIndoorLoc) with different environments and settings. Findings: 1. The conditional entropy increases when modeling more of the environment's uncertainty in the sensor model.; 2. The median location error does not necessarily increase with the median conditional entropy.; 3. Samples with low conditional entropy tend to have low location error, while samples with high conditional entropy can have either low or high location error.; 4. The quality of the sensor model can be estimated by the fraction of validation samples that comply with the relationship between conditional entropy and location error.; 5. The sensor model's performance can be improved by incorporating the antenna gain, using a fixed parameter σ, and increasing the region of reference locations used for training.; 6. The absence of an RSSI value of an access point due to interference is not yet included in the model.; 7. The proposed approach allows for the correct assessment of the uncertainty over the location estimate without requiring a ground truth.. Mechanism: The conditional entropy is calculated from the posterior probability distribution of the locations, which is conditional on the measurement (Wi-Fi fingerprint). The sensor model's quality is related to its ability to capture the uncertainties in the environment, such as the antenna gain and the presence of extra access points.. Limitations: The model does not fully incorporate the situation where an access point is not received due to interference, and the training procedure may not always result in satisfactory values for the parameter σ.. Future work: Creating probabilistic sensor models that not only estimate the location but also correctly indicate the uncertainty of the location estimate, and exploring other sources of uncertainty that can be included in the model.. Quote: "we propose to derive such a measure from the evaluation of the posterior probability distribution over the locations in an environment without the explicit need for a ground truth"

Question: How can a unique five-element Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn high entropy alloy thin film be synthesized in a single step to achieve soft magnetic properties with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity, overcoming the challenges of anomalous deposition and phase control in aqueous media?. System: Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn high entropy alloy (near equi-atomic composition). Processing: Pulse electrodeposition in aqueous medium at ~45 ºC; optimized parameters: forward ON time 50 ms, OFF time 10 ms, applied potential 1.5 V (potentiostatic mode), using sodium citrate as complexing agent and boric acid as buffer.. Test conditions: Room temperature characterization; Magnetic properties measured via Vibrating Sample Magnetometry (VSM) and Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) from 9 to 18 GHz; Microstructure analyzed via FESEM, STEM-EDS, 2D X-ray diffraction, and HRTEM.. Findings: The fabricated Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn HEA thin films exhibited a saturation magnetization (Ms) of ~82 emu/g.; The films showed a relatively low coercivity (Hc) of 19.5 Oe and a remanent magnetization (Mr) of 1.17%.; The alloy hosts nanocrystalline features with a grain size ranging from ~5 to 20 nm.; The films possess a dual-phase structure consisting of Face Centered Cubic (FCC) and Body Centered Cubic (BCC) phases.; FMR measurements yielded a 4πMs value of ~16,136 Oe, indicating potential for microwave device applications.; The composition was found to be uniform throughout the film with no different chemical compositions in FCC and BCC grains.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the soft magnetic behavior and high saturation magnetization to the crystalline nature of the films (FCC/BCC dual phases) and the high concentration of ferromagnetic elements (Fe, Co, Ni) relative to diamagnetic elements (Cu, Zn). The pulse electrodeposition technique controls the reduction of five metal ions uniformly by managing the local pH, minimizing hydroxide formation, and reducing residual stresses, which facilitates the formation of nanocrystalline grains and twins with low stacking fault energy.. Limitations: The text notes that the composition of the HEA thin films varies slightly between STEM-EDS (single location) and FESEM-EDS (multiple locations) due to local heterogeneities and length scale differences, though the overall distribution is confirmed to be within the HEA range.. Future work: The authors propose that additional tuning of the electrodeposition parameters and the relative composition of the constituent elements can further reduce the coercivity of the thin film.. Quote: "The fabricated Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn HEA thin films exhibited high saturation magnetization value of ~ 82 emu/g, relatively low coercivity value of 19.5 Oe and remanent magnetization of 1.17%."

card: Paper card. Question: How does a Permanent Parallel Magnetic Field (PPMF) of 9 T affect the electrodeposition current, mass deposition, and surface morphology of Ni-Co-Fe-Zn quaternary alloys compared to deposition without a magnetic field?. System: Ni-Co-Fe-Zn quaternary alloys deposited from a chloride solution containing 1 M NiCl2·6H2O, 0.25 M CoCl2·6H2O, 0.25 M FeCl2·4H2O, 0.25 M ZnCl2, and 0.5 M H3BO3. Processing: Electrodeposition via chronoamperometry and cyclic voltammetry at -1.1, -1.2, and -1.3 V for 2400 seconds at 30-32°C and pH 4 ± 0.1, with and without a 9 T Permanent Parallel Magnetic Field (PPMF) applied parallel to the cathode surface. Test conditions: Temperature: 30-32°C; pH: 4 ± 0.1; Electrolyte: Chloride bath; Magnetic field: 9 T PPMF parallel to cathode; Duration: 2400 sec; Potentials: -1.1, -1.2, -1.3 V. Findings: The percentage of current enhancement (Γ%) increased with more negative potentials: 11.9% at -1.1 V, 16.7% at -1.2 V, and 18.5% at -1.3 V for a 2400 sec duration.; Surface roughness (RMS) decreased from 48.5 nm to 23 nm at -1.1 V and from 112 nm to 39 nm at -1.3 V when the PPMF was applied.; The limiting current was enhanced in the presence of the PPMF, with current values increasing from 6.7 to 7.5 mA at -1.1 V, 18 to 20 mA at -1.2 V, and 27 to 32 mA at -1.3 V.; The mass of electrodeposition increased with the presence of the PPMF, with the difference in mass deposition ranging from 0.03 to 0.107 mg cm min-1.; The Content of Ni in the electrodeposited layers was always lower than the Composition Reference Line (CRL) due to anomalous behavior.; The lowest elemental content in the deposited layers belonged to Fe due to the chemical oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ in the solution.; The morphology changed from polyhedral grains (without PPMF) to a nodular shape (with PPMF) at -1.10 V.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the increased mass transport and current to the Magneto-Hydrodynamic (MHD) effect, largely caused by the Lorentz Force, which reduces the diffusion layer thickness. They also suggest that the magnetic field suppresses dendritic growth by reducing the effective potential at the tips of dendrites, leading to smoother surfaces.. Limitations: The text notes that the solution was free of chelating reagents, which led to the lowest elemental content being Fe due to oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+, and states that the smoothness effect of an applied magnetic field on electrodeposition surfaces is still unclear.. Quote: "The percentage of current enhancement (Γ%) was increased in the presence of PPMF, with results of Γ% = 11.9%, 16.7% and 18.5% at -1.1, -1.2 and -1.3 V respectively for a 2400 sec duration."
